6. However, against that application, the present opposite party No. 1—plaintiff filed a written objection denying all the material averments so made in the application stating, inter alia, that the application filed under Order VII, rule 11 is totally misconceived and the abuses of the process of the court as the same has been filed only to delay the disposal of the suit. It has further been asserted in the written objection that, the suit has been filed for declaration that, the purported foreign award is a nullity and not binding upon the plaintiff and then implementation of the award through filing money execution case after filing of the suit cannot be allowed which has been filed only to circumvent the decree might have been passed in its favour and the application so filed by the defendant No. 1, is liable to be rejected. However, the said application filed by the present petitioner as defendant No. 1 was taken up for hearing by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st court, Dhaka and vide impugned order dated 25-9-2024 rejected the same holding that, the provision of section 42 of the Arbitration Act is not applicable in rejecting a plaint as that provision does not speak to set-aside any foreign award vis-a-vis apart from the grounds provided in section 46 to the Arbitration Act, 2001, the plaintiff has also taken several other grounds in the plaint challenging the foreign award which cannot be adjudicated without taking evidence from the parties to the suit having no scope to reject the plaint. It is at that stage, the defendant No. 1 in the suit filed this revisional application and obtained instant rule. 

 7. Mr. Syed Emran Hossain, the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner upon taking us to the revisional application at the very outset submits that, the learned judge of the trial court has misconceived innot taking into account of the fact that, the defendant has rightly obtained a foreign award as per clause 13 of the agreement signed by both the plaintiff and defendant dated 1-7-2022 and since the plaintiff had duly been notified before initiating the arbitration proceedings before the Singapore International Arbitration Center (SIAC) in SIAC Arbitration Case No. 032 of 2023, so there has been no scope to say that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 had no knowledge about the continuation and passing the said award. To supplement the said submission, the learned counsel then contends that, after passing the award, by a foreign tribunal, the plaintiff opposite party have two options either to pray for setting aside the award under the provision of section 24 of International Arbitration Act, 1994 (a statute of the Republic of Singapore) and secondly, challenge the award in the execution case when the award winning party will file for its recognition and enforcement before the District Judge under section 45 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 having no scope to challenge the award by filing a separate suit in an ordinary civil court. To fortify the said submission, the learned counsel then referred the provision of section 42 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and submits that an aggrieved party against whom an award is given can pray for set-aside such award by filing a Miscellaneous Case under that provision in case of domestic Arbitration to the District Judge and that of International Commercial Arbitration in the High Court Division held in Bangladesh where there is not provision to challenge a foreign award under section 42 of the Act which alternatively denotes, there has been implied legal bar to challenge any foreign award under section 42 and therefore the petitioner has rightly filed the application under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure on relying upon the provision provided in section 9 of the Code of Civil procedure. 

 8. The learned counsel further contends that since the petitioner has already filed money execution case No. 25 of 2024 on 1-7-2024 before the District Judge, Dhaka for recognition and enforcement of the award, so the plaintiff opposite party has every scope to make its all grievences by filing an application under section 46 of the Arbitration Act but without doing so, the opposite party filed a civil suit challenging a foreign award which is totally bar under the provision of section 42 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. 

 12. The learned counsel further contends that, since the present opposite party had ample opportunity either to challenge the award before the tribunal where arbitration was held or to challenge it by filing an application under section 46 of the Act to the District Judge, Dhaka before recognition and enforcement of the award obtained by the present petitioner, so the suit cannot be proceeded with. However, in support of his submission, the learned counsel has placed his reliance in the decision reported in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4 and read out the relevant ratio settled therein. The learned counsel next contends that, though that very ratio has been settled in an award passed by an International Commercial tribunal where a defeating party to the award without taking resort to the provision of section 42 of the Act filed a suit in an ordinary civil court for setting aside the award when their lordships ultimately found that under no circumstances can an award be it passed by a domestic or International commercial tribunal be called in question by filing a suit in a civil court. But the case in hand, rather stands in better footing since the award in question is a foreign one passed by a foreign tribunal and since there has been no provision in section 42 of the Act even to challenge such award, so it turns out that the legislature in a conscious manner put an implied bar to challenge such award passed by a foreign arbitral tribunal by filing a suit in an ordinary civil court and finally prays for making the rule absolute. 

 14. The learned counsel in his second leg of submission then contends that, since section 42 of the Arbitration Act does not speak about setting aside a foreign award, so the plaintiffs opposite party No. 1 has got no other option but to challenge a foreign award by filing a civil suit for setting aside the same and the plaintiff-opposite party has thus rightly filed a civil suit to that effect. Giving reference to the decision referred by the learned counsel for the petitioner reported in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4, the learned counsel contends that, since that very decision has been passed basing on an award held in this country in an International Commercial Arbitration, so that judgment is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case in particular, in rejecting a plaint. Drawing our attention to the provision of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned counsel further contends that, since from the plaint it does not show, it is impliedly bar, by any law, so rule 11(d) of order 7 of the Code or Civil Procedure will not be applicable here. Today, the learned counsel by filing a supplementary-counter-affidavit and by annexing a good number of documents tried to impress us that the petitioner had earlier filed similar application (under order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure) in title suit No. 435 of 2022 which was rejected on 29-5-2024 and then filed another application under section 7 and 10 of the Arbitration Act, for staying further proceedings of the said suit which was also rejected on 25-9-2024. Apart from that, it also contested First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 57 of 2023 which stemmed from an order dated 2-10-2022 passed by the trial curt rejecting an application for temporary injunction brought by the present opposite party and even contested the appeal before the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1958 of 2023 which was also disposed of on 24-7-2023 and of 21-1-2024 so in spite of having every knowledge about the award passed in its favour dated 24-1-2024, the petitioner for the first time disclosed such award only when they filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Title Suit No. 435 of 2022 and soon after coming to learn about getting such award this plaintiff filed Title suit No. 371 of 2024 on 14-5-2024 and only after that, the petitioner filed Money Execution Case No. 25 of 2024 on 1-7-2024 so considering all these material facts, this Hon'ble Court may discharge the rule. 

 17. On careful perusal of section 42 we find that there have been two options opened for a defeating party to the award to challenge an award seeking setting aside of the same that is, if an award is passed in an ordinary domestic arbitration to be challenged before a District Judge and an award given in an International Commercial arbitration held in Bangladesh to the High Court Division. So, clearly, there is nothing in section 42 of the Act for setting aside any foreign award held at any tribunal outside of our country. The learned judge of the trial court held that since there has been no provision to challenge a foreign award in section 42 of the Act so the suit can continue. But he despondently failed to comprehend that section 42 is totally silent to challenge a foreign award, so the legislature put an emplied bar in setting aside it under Arbitration Act let alone by filing a fresh suit. So, the alleged assertion taken by the trial court on that simple point clearly exemplifies his lack of legal acumen. It is the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner that since section 42 of the Act is silent about setting aside a foreign award so it alternatively proves that there has been a legal bar and that bar has to be inferred as of implied bar within the mischief of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that connection, the learned counsel contends that Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure does not provide about implied or express bar rather speaks "barred by law" so the plaint can be rejected under clause (d) of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. We find ample substance to the said submission, because the legislature has rightly and very consciously omitted to challenge a foreign award under section 42 of the Act if not filing a civil suit. 

 18. Then again, in an effort to enforce the award granted in favour of the petitioner, it filed a Money Execution Case No. 25 of 2024 on 1-7-2024 before the District Judge, Dhaka under section 45 of the Arbitration Act. Now let us reproduce section 45 of the Act, here for our better understanding: 

 19. From the plain reading of the title of section 45 of the Act, we find that there have been two schemes in that section, that is, a foreign award has to be recognized first and if the award winning party can over come such recognition, then the enforcement of that foreign award will come. We have been informed by the learned counsel for the petitioner that the hearing on recognition of the foreign award has not yet been held and he next submits that, the plaintiff-opposite party has thus ample opportunity to file written objection either against that Money Execution Case or file an application before the executing court invoking the provision of section 46 of the Act where different grounds have been set out for negating the recognition of the award like section 43 of the Act. The said submission has got material substance in the context that section 42 does not provide any provision for setting aside any 'foreign award` so the scope of the plaintiff is now confined only to file an application whatever form in be in the Money Execution Case for not recognizing the award and if the award is not recognized and enforced, the petitioner can then avail the option to prefer appeal under section 48 of the Act. Overall, it turns out that the opposite party has the remedy in section 45 of the Act. 

 22. Since in the four corner of the Arbitration Act, 2001 there has been no express bar to file a suit challenging any award given by a domestic tribunal in an ordinary Arbitration or International commercial Arbitration let alone any award of a foreign tribunal so, filing a civil suit for setting aside an award will definitely be regarded as implied bar as has been stated above. That very proposition has already been settled in the decision by our Appellate Division in a case reported in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4. Their lordships amongst others held that: 

 23. The said decision is squarely applicable in the fact and circumstances of the instant case because when a domestic award cannot be challenged by filing a civil suit then no question can at all arise to challenge a foreign award in an ordinary civil court. On top of that, in our country, a District Judge is the highest seat of judiciary in our subordinate judiciary who has been assigned with the ordinary jurisdiction in all sorts of arbitral dispute save for International commercial dispute. An award given by a tribunal even comprising any former Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh is subject to challenge before a District Judge under section 42 and 43 of the Arbitration Act. Now if an avenue is opened to challenge an award let alone a foreign award to a Joint District Judge, subordinate to District Judge, it would be a mockery for establishing Arbitration Tribunal if not their award and for that obvious reason, it has been set at rest once for all in the decision by our Appellate Division in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4. 

 24. At this, the learned counsel for the opposite party has vehemently submits that, since there has been bar in section 42 of the Act vis-a-vis on the face of the plaint to challenge an award so the plaint cannot be rejected. But from the foregoing discussion and observation, it is now crystal clear that everything needs not be disclosed in a statute which some time has to be deduced from the scheme of a certain statute. Last but not the least, though the learned counsel for the opposite party No. 1 has referred a slew of decisions even passed by our Appellate Division but the facts so have been described in those very decisions is totally distinguishable with the facts and circumstances of the instant case because the award is given in view of an agreed agreement by the parties which can well be amenable under Arbitration Act, 2001 but those have totally been absent in all the decisions cited by the learned counsel for the opposite party No. 1 rather the decision cited and reported in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4 can be taken as a milestone to be followed by us not to challenge an award to any ordinary civil court. Though in the application so filed under Order VII, rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, we find in paragraph No. 8, that the learned Advocate before the trial court has also referred the said decision by our Appellate Division but the learned Joint District Judge even did not bother to take into account of the decision and very abruptly passed a judgment giving two absurd reasoning, which is totally beyond the scheme of law and thus the learned Joint District Judge is hereby cautioned not to venture into such kinds of misdoing in future when a judgment of his apex court will be placed.
